title: A/B Testing and Business Metrics
summary: A/B testing is how data-driven companies make decisions: instead of guessing whether a new button, price, or feature is better, they run a controlled experiment. Users are randomly split into a control group (current version, A) and a treatment group
content:
# A/B Testing and Business Metrics ##### The winning test that lost ₹40 lakh A food delivery app in Gurugram tested a redesigned restaurant listing. After five days, the treatment group showed 8.2% more orders. The team declared a win and rolled it out to everyone. Revenue fell 3% over the following quarter. Two things had gone wrong. They had been checking results daily and stopped on the first day the difference looked significant — a practice that inflates the false-positive rate from 5% to well over 25%. And their primary metric was *order count*, while the redesign had quietly pushed users toward cheaper restaurants. More orders, smaller baskets, less revenue. Both errors are avoidable and both are extremely common. A/B testing is how data-driven companies decide what to ship, and doing it badly is worse than not doing it — because a bad test produces confident wrong conclusions rather than honest uncertainty. ##### Why experiments beat analysis Observational data tells you what correlates. An experiment tells you what *causes*. The reason is randomisation. If you randomly assign users to two groups, the groups are on average identical in every respect — age, city, past behaviour, and every variable you never thought to measure. Any difference in outcome must therefore be caused by the treatment. This is why "users who used feature X retained better, so let's push feature X" is unreliable. Users who chose to use X were already different. Randomised assignment breaks that link. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[All eligible users] --> B{Random assignment} B -->|50%| C[Control A: current version] B -->|50%| D[Treatment B: new version] C --> E[Measure primary metric] D --> F[Measure primary metric] E --> G{Difference larger than
random variation?} F --> G G -->|Yes, and guardrails OK| H[Ship it] G -->|No| I[Do not ship - or the test was underpowered] ``` ##### Designing the experiment Five decisions, all made *before* any data is collected. **1. The hypothesis.** Specific, directional, and falsifiable. Weak: "The new design will be better." Strong: "Showing delivery time estimates on the listing page will increase order conversion rate by at least 3% relative, because uncertainty about delivery time is a stated reason for abandonment." Naming the mechanism matters. It forces you to think about *why* the change should work, which tells you what secondary metrics to watch. **2. The randomisation unit.** Almost always the **user**, not the session or the page view. Randomising per request means the same person sees both versions, contaminating the comparison and making any per-user metric meaningless. ```python import hashlib def assign_variant(user_id: str, experiment: str, split: float = 0.5) -> str: """Deterministic, salted — same user always gets the same variant.""" h = hashlib.sha256(f"{experiment}:{user_id}".encode()).hexdigest() bucket = int(h[:12], 16) / float(16 ** 12) return "treatment" if bucket < split else "control" ``` Salting with the experiment name is essential. Without it, the same users land in the same bucket across every experiment, so effects correlate across tests and an unlucky user is unlucky in all of them. **3. Metrics, in three tiers.** | Tier | Purpose | Example | |---|---|---| | **Primary (OEC)** | The single decision metric | Revenue per user | | **Secondary** | Explain *why* the primary moved | Conversion rate, average order value, items viewed | | **Guardrail** | Must not degrade | p95 latency, error rate, unsubscribe rate, support tickets | **Choose exactly one primary metric, before launch.** Tracking five and declaring victory on whichever moved is post-hoc selection, and it is how teams "win" every test while the business does not improve. The Gurugram failure was a primary metric error. Order count went up; revenue per user went down. Choosing revenue per user as the OEC would have caught it immediately. Guardrails are what stop a winning test from being a disaster. An aggressive notification change that lifts engagement 6% while doubling unsubscribes is a loss. **4. Sample size.** Compute it in advance. ```python from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize import numpy as np def sample_size_proportion(baseline, mde_relative, alpha=0.05, power=0.80): """Users needed PER GROUP to detect a relative lift.""" effect = proportion_effectsize(baseline * (1 + mde_relative), baseline) return int(np.ceil(NormalIndPower().solve_power( effect_size=effect, alpha=alpha, power=power, ratio=1.0))) for mde in [0.20, 0.10, 0.05, 0.03]: n = sample_size_proportion(baseline=0.042, mde_relative=mde) print(f"detect {mde:.0%} relative lift -> {n:,} users per group") # detect 20% lift -> 2,278 per group # detect 10% lift -> 9,047 per group # detect 5% lift -> 36,000 per group # detect 3% lift -> 99,760 per group ``` Note the shape: **sample size scales with 1/MDE².** Halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the users required. This is why small effects need enormous traffic, and why "we ran it for a week and saw nothing" often means the test never had a chance. **Statistical power** is the probability of detecting a real effect. The 80% convention means you miss one real effect in five. The Gurugram test at 900 users per group had roughly 15% power for their target effect — it was inconclusive before it started. **5. Duration.** Run at least one full weekly cycle, because weekday and weekend behaviour differ sharply. In India, avoid straddling a festival period — Diwali week is not representative of anything. Then run until you hit the pre-computed sample size, and stop. ##### Analysing the results Before any statistics, run the sanity check. ```python from scipy import stats import pandas as pd def srm_check(n_control, n_treatment, expected_split=0.5): """Sample Ratio Mismatch — the FIRST thing to check.""" total = n_control + n_treatment expected = [total * (1 - expected_split), total * expected_split] chi2, p = stats.chisquare([n_control, n_treatment], expected) print(f"split: {n_control:,} / {n_treatment:,} p = {p:.4f}") if p < 0.001: print(" ⚠ SRM DETECTED — assignment or logging is broken. " "Do NOT analyse this experiment.") return p >= 0.001 ``` If you configured a 50/50 split and observed 50.8/49.2 with a large sample, that is statistically impossible by chance. It means your assignment, logging or filtering has a bug — perhaps the treatment version crashes for some users, who then never appear in the data. **A failed SRM check invalidates the experiment entirely.** Fix it and rerun. Then the test itself: ```python import numpy as np from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest, confint_proportions_2indep def analyse_proportion_test(c_conv, c_n, t_conv, t_n, alpha=0.05): p_c, p_t = c_conv / c_n, t_conv / t_n stat, pval = proportions_ztest([t_conv, c_conv], [t_n, c_n]) lo, hi = confint_proportions_2indep(t_conv, t_n, c_conv, c_n, method="wald", alpha=alpha) return { "control_rate": round(p_c, 4), "treatment_rate": round(p_t, 4), "absolute_lift_pp": round((p_t - p_c) * 100, 3), "relative_lift_pct": round((p_t - p_c) / p_c * 100, 2), "ci_absolute": (round(lo * 100, 3), round(hi * 100, 3)), "p_value": round(pval, 5), "significant": pval < alpha, } print(analyse_proportion_test(c_conv=1_512, c_n=36_000, t_conv=1_648, t_n=36_000)) ``` For continuous metrics like revenue per user, use Welch's t-test: ```python t_stat, p = stats.ttest_ind(treatment_revenue, control_revenue, equal_var=False) diff = treatment_revenue.mean() - control_revenue.mean() se = np.sqrt(treatment_revenue.var(ddof=1)/len(treatment_revenue) + control_revenue.var(ddof=1)/len(control_revenue)) print(f"lift ₹{diff:.2f}, 95% CI [₹{diff-1.96*se:.2f}, ₹{diff+1.96*se:.2f}], p={p:.4f}") ``` **Always report the confidence interval, not just the p-value.** "Lift +1.2% (95% CI: −0.4% to +2.8%), p = 0.14" is honest and actionable. "Not significant" discards the information that the effect is probably positive and the test simply lacked power. Revenue metrics have heavy right tails, which inflates variance and destroys power. Two standard remedies: winsorise extreme values at the 99th percentile, and use **CUPED**, which regresses out each user's pre-experiment behaviour: ```python def cuped(y_post, y_pre): theta = np.cov(y_post, y_pre)[0, 1] / np.var(y_pre) return y_post - theta * (y_pre - y_pre.mean()) ``` CUPED typically cuts variance by 30–50%, equivalent to running the test 1.5–2× longer, for free. ##### Business metrics worth knowing The metric you optimise shapes the product, so choosing well matters more than the statistics. | Metric | Definition | Watch for | |---|---|---| | **Conversion rate** | Converters / visitors | Which conversion? Define it precisely | | **Retention (D1/D7/D30)** | Still active after N days | The clearest signal of real value | | **ARPU** | Revenue / active users | Heavy-tailed; needs large samples | | **AOV** | Revenue / orders | Can rise while total revenue falls | | **LTV** | Total value over the relationship | Estimated, not measured — treat with care | | **Churn rate** | Leavers / total in a period | The inverse of retention | | **NPS** | Promoters − detractors | Response bias is severe | Two traps. **Ratio metrics can move in misleading ways** — AOV rising because low-value customers left is not a win. And **short-term metrics can conflict with long-term health**: aggressive notifications lift weekly engagement and depress 90-day retention. This is why guardrails and holdback groups matter. A **long-term holdback** — keeping 1–5% of users on the old version for months after rollout — is the only reliable way to detect effects that decay or reverse. ##### The pitfalls **Peeking** is the one that would have saved Gurugram ₹40 lakh, and it deserves a demonstration rather than an assertion: ```python rng = np.random.default_rng(42) false_positives_fixed = 0 false_positives_peeking = 0 n_sims, n_per_group, checks = 1000, 10_000, 20 for _ in range(n_sims): # NO real effect — both groups identical c = rng.binomial(1, 0.042, n_per_group) t = rng.binomial(1, 0.042, n_per_group) # Correct: test once at the end _, p_final = proportions_ztest([t.sum(), c.sum()], [n_per_group, n_per_group]) false_positives_fixed += p_final < 0.05 # Peeking: check 20 times, stop at the first significant result for step in np.linspace(n_per_group // checks, n_per_group, checks, dtype=int): _, p = proportions_ztest([t[:step].sum(), c[:step].sum()], [step, step]) if p < 0.05: false_positives_peeking += 1 break print(f"fixed horizon: {false_positives_fixed / n_sims:.1%} false positives") print(f"peeking: {false_positives_peeking / n_sims:.1%} false positives") # fixed horizon: 5.1% # peeking: 28.4% ``` Run that yourself. Seeing 28% where the theory promises 5% is far more convincing than being told. The fix is either a fixed sample size decided in advance, or a **sequential test** (mSPRT, always-valid confidence sequences) designed for continuous monitoring. The other pitfalls: - **Multiple comparisons.** Twenty metrics at α = 0.05 gives a 64% chance of at least one false positive. Apply Benjamini-Hochberg, or commit to one primary metric. - **Novelty and primacy effects.** Users react to change itself. Check whether the effect decays over the test period; if week two is flat, it was novelty. - **Simpson's paradox.** Treatment wins in every segment but loses overall, because the segment mix differs. Check segment balance. - **Network interference.** In marketplaces, treatment and control compete for the same supply, so treating one group affects the other. Geo or cluster randomisation is needed. - **Selection bias.** Analysing only users who completed the flow excludes those the treatment drove away. Analyse by assignment (intent to treat), not by exposure. ##### Bandits, briefly An A/B test sends half your traffic to a losing variant for the whole duration — that is the cost of learning. **Multi-armed bandits** adapt allocation toward better-performing arms as evidence accumulates. Use bandits when the reward is fast, you have many variants, and minimising regret matters (email subject lines, creative selection). Use A/B tests when you need a clean, defensible causal estimate of effect size, or the metric is delayed. **Bandits optimise; A/B tests measure.** A common hybrid uses a bandit to narrow ten candidates to two, then a proper A/B between them. ##### Common mistakes - Peeking daily with a fixed-horizon test. - More than one primary metric, chosen after seeing results. - No SRM check, so broken assignment goes undetected. - Randomising per session instead of per user. - Running four days and missing the weekly cycle. - Computing power after the test instead of before. - Reporting p-values with no confidence interval or effect size. - Ignoring guardrails when the primary metric wins. - Analysing only exposed users rather than all assigned users. - Optimising a proxy metric that diverges from business value. ##### Hands-on Design an A/B test for a hypothetical product change: state a directional hypothesis with a mechanism, define one primary metric plus three secondary and four guardrail metrics, and compute the required sample size for a realistic MDE at 80% power. Then simulate data under two scenarios — a true 5% lift and no effect at all — and verify your analysis correctly distinguishes them. Run the peeking simulation above and report your own false-positive rate. For the mini-project, analyse an A/B test dataset end to end. Start with the SRM check. Then run the appropriate test for your metric type, report absolute and relative lift with confidence intervals, break results down by two segments to check for heterogeneity and Simpson's paradox, verify the effect is stable across the test period rather than decaying, and check every guardrail. Finish with a business-facing recommendation of no more than 150 words that states the decision, the expected impact with its uncertainty range, and any caveat a decision-maker needs to know. For the assignment, explain with a worked example why peeking leads to false positives. Use your own simulation numbers rather than quoting the theory — the gap between 5% and 28% is the argument, and having generated it yourself makes it yours. ##### Key takeaways - Randomisation is what turns correlation into causation; assign per user with a salted hash, deterministically. - Choose one primary metric before launch — order count rose while revenue fell, and that is a metric-selection failure. - Sample size scales with 1/MDE²; compute it in advance, and never stop early because it looks good. - Run the SRM check first — a broken split invalidates the entire experiment regardless of the result. - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals, enforce guardrails, and watch for novelty effects and Simpson's paradox.
